title: We’re Obsessed with Controlling Student Thinking
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Dempsey opens a series arguing that the growing demand for students to submit chat logs, document their process and keep transparency journals is metacognition turned into control. He reconstructs the logic: since teachers cannot control AI-generated products, they exert more control over the process. He compares it to the Steve Martin scene in The Jerk where the character keeps finding one more thing he needs. He says the approach will fail because of three misunderstandings: thinking is internal and messy, so prompts do not capture it; effective AI collaboration looks rambling and incoherent from outside; and teachers have no training or rubric to assess chat logs. He distinguishes this from his earlier thesis that metacognitive questions are for students, not for teachers to inspect, and promises to unpack each point and offer alternatives.
points: Demanding chat logs and process journals gives up control of the product only to tighten control of the student's process.
Student prompts cannot capture thinking because thinking is internal, messy, half-baked and often emotional.
Effective AI collaboration can look unstable and incoherent in a transcript, so the log is a poor measure of quality.
Teachers have no rubric, exemplars or time to assess chat logs, so the system collects information nobody knows what to do with.
His earlier thesis stands as the contrast: metacognitive questions are for the students' benefit, not for teacher surveillance.
quotes: The questions are for the students. We don’t need to see how students respond to them. Merely asking them is enough to get students to begin surfacing the types of thinking patterns that will benefit their work generally and their collaboration with AI more specifically.

First, this isn’t how people actually think. By its very nature, thinking happens internally. Thinking is an internal process that precedes external action. It is messy, typically half-baked, often emotional.

Second, it isn’t how students should use AI. I will guarantee you that if I submitted my chat logs to you, you would have me committed. My prompts are rambling. Incoherent. Filled with typos. Often less-than-flattering superlatives. By any measure, I’m unstable and ineffective. But that doesn’t mean my collaboration with AI isn’t working.

Third, we wouldn’t know what to do with this information anyway. Seriously, suddenly we’re experts in assessing AI-chat logs??? For real?! And, now we have the time and training to comb through 12 pages of one sentence prompts from students alongside GPT’s rather uneconomical replies? And what’s the rubric on that? Where’s the exemplar for thought that is by design tentative, iterative, recursive, and emergent?
Students, forced to comply, will do exactly what’s expected in the exact form they expect we expect. We know how this goes. And it doesn’t go well.
